card: Why 38°C on the coast can be more dangerous than 44°C inland — and why no Indian criterion counts it.

frame.alt: A line of women in headscarves and long skirts standing across a stony hillside yard, each holding a bulky sack of pale straw substrate against her chest, a heap of filled sacks on a blue tarpaulin on the ground in front of them and a bare-branched tree and steep Himalayan slopes behind

answer: Apparent temperature is what heat does to a body once humidity is taken into account, rather than what a thermometer reads in the shade. It matters because humans cool by evaporating sweat, and humid air stops that working. India has no notified threshold for it, so nothing can be over the limit — but across the stations this site reads, it is rising at more of them than the dry-bulb maximum is.
explainHead: Why the thermometer is not the measurement
explainLead: A thermometer measures air. A person is a wet object trying to lose heat into it.
explain: The body's main defence against heat is evaporation. Sweat leaves the skin, takes latent heat with it, and the skin cools. How fast that happens depends on how much more water vapour the surrounding air can hold — so in dry air evaporation is efficient and in saturated air it barely happens at all.

The consequence is that two days at the same dry-bulb temperature are not the same day. A 44°C afternoon in Jodhpur at fifteen per cent humidity is survivable for a body that can drink; a 38°C afternoon in Kolkata at eighty per cent may not be, because there is nowhere for the sweat to go. Apparent temperature — sometimes published as heat index or feels-like — combines the two into one figure.

India's own national heat product agrees with this in its design. Two of its four layers add moisture rather than reporting temperature alone, which is independent evidence that dry-bulb maximum was never the right single measure.

defs.d: Air temperature as an ordinary thermometer reads it. What IMD's heatwave criteria use.
Temperature adjusted for humidity — closer to physiological load. No Indian threshold is set against it.
A related and stricter measure: the lowest temperature reachable by evaporation. Above about 35°C sustained, no amount of sweating is enough.

after: Read the first pair against the second. Peak apparent temperature rises at more stations than it falls at; the dry-bulb maximum splits evenly. The measure that captures what a body experiences is moving, and the measure the criteria are written on is not.

Because nothing is notified against it, apparent temperature is counted on this site as itself and never marked as a breach. That is a deliberate restriction: a reading is only shown against a limit where a limit exists, and inventing one to make a chart legible would be the same error the fire and rainfall pages refuse.

readHead: How to read a feels-like figure
readLead: It is a model of a body, and different publishers model a different body.
measure: Which formula? Heat index, humidex, apparent temperature and wet-bulb globe temperature are four different constructions with different assumptions about shade, wind and clothing. They do not agree and should not be mixed in one series.
Shade or sun? Most feels-like figures assume shade. Direct sun adds several degrees to the load and is not in the number.
Whose body? These indices are built for a healthy adult at rest. A construction worker, an infant and someone on medication that suppresses sweating are all outside the assumption.
Modelled, always. Apparent temperature is computed from temperature and humidity, never measured directly — so it inherits the uncertainty of both, and fails the way a model fails.
cannot: It cannot be compared with a dry-bulb reading. They are different quantities and only one has a legal threshold.
It cannot be used to declare a heatwave in India. The criteria are dry-bulb, and a declaration is a defined administrative act.
It cannot account for night-time recovery, which is a separate and arguably larger part of the danger — see warm nights.
A reanalysis smooths local extremes hardest at exactly the tail this measure lives in, and carries no urban heat island.
